how-much-to-charge-to-install-crown-mold.text:
← Crown molding bid calculator

How much to charge to install crown molding

Finish carpenters get shopped on a published $8 a foot installed crown Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the grade or the extras. 80 lf of paint-grade simple cove in one 8-ft room is a different job from 80 lf of stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story foyer with 14 coped insides and an LED cove.

Open the free crown molding bid calculator

Price the run and the extras, not the $8/ft dump

A crown-molding install is a run, then a grade, then how much of that run is actually sold. Paint-grade is miters, caulk, then paint. Stain-grade insides are coped. Simple cove is the cheap special. Colonial is more cuts. Built-up is two or three stacked pieces. Flat 8-ft is the cheap-special assumption. A cathedral or tray changes the spring angle. A two-story foyer is a scaffold ticket.

Paint-grade cove is not a stain-grade foyer

The cheap special is almost always 80 lf of paint-grade simple cove, eight insides, one 8-ft room, no demo, no LED. A stain-grade built-up foyer is a different crew day. Matching a per-foot number on a foyer job is how a sold crown job becomes a loss when the corners and the access eat the margin.

This is not painting, drywall, or plantation shutters

Interior painting is a coat on walls. Drywall is gypsum hang-and-finish. Cabinet refinishing is doors. Popcorn-ceiling is a scrape and skim. Plantation shutters are louvered panels in an opening. This prices a crown-molding run: linear feet, corners, grade, profile, and extras.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the crown molding bid calculator. See also: should I charge $8 a foot for crown molding? and should I match a cheaper quote on a stain-grade job? It is not a millwork shop drawing, a structural opinion, a paint specification, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install crown molding?

Charge from linear feet, corners, grade, profile, and extras — not a published $8-a-foot special. 80 lf of paint-grade simple cove in one 8-ft room is a different job from 80 lf of stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story foyer with 14 coped insides and an LED cove.

Is paint-grade the same bid as stain-grade?

No. Paint-grade is miters, caulk, then paint. Stain-grade insides are coped and the stock costs more — there is no caulk hiding a bad joint. Matching a paint-grade special on a stain-grade foyer is how a sold crown job becomes a loss when the corners and the access eat the margin.

How do corners, a foyer, and an LED cove change a crown price?

Inside corners are copes on stain-grade and miters on paint-grade. A cathedral or tray ceiling changes the spring angle. A two-story foyer is a scaffold ticket. Demo, blocking, an LED cove, and matching existing casing do not live in a published per-foot special.

Is this the same as painting, drywall, or plantation shutters?

No. Interior painting is a coat on walls. Drywall is gypsum hang-and-finish. Cabinet refinishing is doors. Popcorn-ceiling is a scrape and skim. Plantation shutters are louvered panels in an opening. This prices a crown-molding run: linear feet, corners, grade, profile, and extras.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why can a competitor advertise “$8 a foot installed”?

    Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: 80 linear feet of paint-grade simple cove, 8 inside corners, one flat 8-ft room. It really does price low. What the per-foot number cannot see is grade, profile, ceiling type, ceiling height, corners, and extras like demo, blocking, an LED cove, or matching existing casing. Price your actual room beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

    Why does stain-grade cost more than paint-grade for the same linear footage?

    Because caulk can hide a rough miter and paint-grade relies on it. Stain-grade crown has to be coped at every inside corner — cut to fit the exact profile of the adjoining piece — because there is no caulk line to hide a gap once it is stained instead of painted. Coping takes longer per corner than caulking a mitered paint-grade joint, and that time is billed per inside corner, not folded into the linear-foot rate.

    Why does a two-story foyer change the price so much for similar linear footage?

    Because the access, not the crown, is the job. A standard 8-ft ceiling only needs a ladder. A 9–10 ft ceiling needs stilts or a rolling scaffold. A two-story foyer needs scaffolding built and moved around the room, which adds hours that have nothing to do with how many feet of crown are going up once the crew is finally standing at the right height.

    Why are inside and outside corners counted separately from linear feet?

    Because coping or mitering a corner takes a fixed amount of time per corner, independent of how long the runs on either side of it are. A short run with 14 corners can take longer than a long run with two. Cathedral and tray ceilings add their own hours on top — a cathedral ceiling changes the spring angle at every cut, and a tray or coffered ceiling adds extra returns and steps that a flat-ceiling rate does not include.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your room dimensions, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — linear feet, corners, ceiling and height extras, demo, blocking, LED cove, and casing match — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

Should I charge $8 a foot for crown molding?

A homeowner brings you a published “$8 a foot installed crown” Facebook special. It reads like a safe number for any run. Priced at this calculator's own default crew rates — a $42 wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin — it does not cover the walk-away price on any of the four jobs the calculator ships with, and the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive is not small.

Open the free crown molding bid calculator

$8/ft is short on every scope, not just the hard ones

Using the calculator's own default crew rates on its four preset jobs, each quoted at $8 a foot on its own linear footage:

JobLinear feet$8/ft quoteWalk-away priceShortfall
Cheap special: paint-grade simple cove, 8 insides, one flat 8-ft room80$640.00$1,182.95$542.95
Typical colonial: paint-grade, 16 insides, 3 rooms180$1,440.00$3,302.54$1,862.54
Stain dining: stain-grade colonial, tray ceiling, 10-ft120$960.00$4,947.07$3,987.07
Losing job: stain-grade built-up, cathedral foyer, LED cove80$640.00$7,710.87$7,070.87

$8/ft never breaks even here, but it does not fail by the same amount twice. It is worth naming because it is the sharpest comparison in the table: the cheap special and the losing job are the same 80 linear feet. Grade, profile, ceiling, and access alone turn a $542.95 shortfall into a $7,070.87 one — thirteen times worse on identical footage.

Same footage, thirteen times the gap

A per-foot number moves in a straight line with linear feet: it cannot see grade, profile, ceiling shape, or how you reach the crown. The walk-away price moves with all four. 80 lf of paint-grade simple cove in a flat 8-ft room copes nothing and climbs no scaffold. The same 80 lf of stain-grade built-up in a two-story cathedral foyer with an LED cove is coped insides, two stacked pieces of stock, a spring-angle change, a scaffold ticket, and an LED channel — none of which a per-foot dump ever carried.

This is a scope question, not a footage question

The trap is not "the run got longer." It is "the run stayed the same length and the owner is asking for stain-grade built-up in a foyer instead of paint-grade cove in a bedroom, and the number I quoted from never had that scope in it." A carpenter who matches the Facebook special on footage alone — without re-checking grade, profile, ceiling, and height — is the one who finds out the copes and the scaffold ate the whole margin.

How to use the comparison

Open the crown molding bid calculator, load the matching starting job from the "Choose a starting job…" preset list, and put the owner's per-foot number (times your linear feet) into "price you're considering." The calculator scores it against the walk-away price for the scope you actually priced, not the scope the flyer was written for.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install crown molding and this calculator vs. Jobber. It is not a millwork shop drawing, a structural opinion, a paint specification, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

Should I charge $8 a foot for crown molding?

No, not at professional crew rates. Under this calculator's own default crew rates ($42/hour wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin), $8 a foot does not cover the walk-away price on any of its four example jobs — not even the cheapest one. On 80 linear feet of paint-grade simple cove in one flat 8-ft room, $8/ft ($640.00) is $542.95 under the $1,182.95 walk-away price.

Why is the gap so much bigger on some jobs than others?

Because $8 a foot is quoted from the linear footage alone, and the walk-away price is not. On the identical 80 linear feet, swapping paint-grade simple cove in a flat room for stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story cathedral foyer with an LED cove raises the walk-away price from $1,182.95 to $7,710.87 — the same $640.00 quote goes from $542.95 short to $7,070.87 short, thirteen times worse on the same footage.

Does a bigger run mean a smaller gap?

No. 180 linear feet of paint-grade colonial ($1,440.00 at $8/ft) is $1,862.54 short of its $3,302.54 walk-away price, and 120 linear feet of stain-grade colonial in a tray ceiling ($960.00 at $8/ft) is $3,987.07 short of its $4,947.07 walk-away price. The shortfall tracks grade, profile, ceiling, and height, not linear feet alone.

should-i-match-a-cheaper-quote-on-a-stai.text:
← Crown molding bid calculator

Should I match a cheaper quote on a stain-grade job?

A homeowner holds a competitor's number and asks you to match it. The number is almost never a lie — it is almost always priced for a different job. A per-foot quote written around 80 lf of paint-grade simple cove in one flat 8-ft room and the same 80 lf as stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story cathedral foyer with an LED cove are, at this calculator's own default crew rates, a $1,182.95 job and a $7,710.87 job. Matching the first number on the second job is not a discount. It is $6,527.92 of work the competitor's number never carried.

Open the free crown molding bid calculator

The trap: matching the number, not the scope

Nobody hands over a quote that says "priced for paint-grade cove in a flat room." They hand over a total, or a per-foot rate. If your job is stain-grade, coped, in a foyer, with an LED cove, the competitor's number and your job can share every dimension — same linear feet, same room count — and still not be the same job. The two figures that actually tell you whether you can match it are the walk-away price for the scope in front of you, and the extra-work share: how much of the crew's time is corners, ceiling, access, demo, blocking, LED, and casing rather than the base run.

Same 80 feet, a 3-in-1 hour swing

Using the calculator's own default crew rates ($42 wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin) on its four preset jobs:

JobLinear feetWalk-away priceExtra-work share of hours
Cheap special: paint-grade simple cove, 8 insides, one flat 8-ft room80$1,182.9521.4%
Typical colonial: paint-grade, 16 insides, 3 rooms180$3,302.5420.6%
Stain dining: stain-grade colonial, tray ceiling, 10-ft120$4,947.0748.6%
Losing job: stain-grade built-up, cathedral foyer, LED cove80$7,710.8760.2%

The cheap special and the losing job are the same 80 linear feet. A per-foot price can only move with that one number, so it treats both rows the same. The extra-work share does not: it climbs from 21.4% of crew hours to 60.2% on the identical footage, because coped inside corners, a cathedral spring angle, a scaffold ticket, demo, blocking, an LED channel, and a casing match are all billed by the job, not by the foot. That is the $6,527.92 a matched per-foot number never had a line item for.

What to do instead of matching the number

Ask what the competitor's quote actually describes — grade, profile, ceiling, corners, access, and extras — before deciding whether to match it. Open the crown molding bid calculator, load the preset closest to your real scope (or build it from your own linear feet, corners, grade, profile, ceiling, height, and extras), and read the walk-away price and the extra-work share for the job you are actually pricing. If the competitor's number sits below your walk-away price for that scope, it was priced for a different job, not a better crew. Copy bid summary turns the scope-aware price into a plain-text draft that names the grade, profile, and extras, so the conversation with the homeowner is about scope rather than about whether your price is fair.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install crown molding and should I charge $8 a foot for crown molding? It is not a millwork shop drawing, a structural opinion, a paint specification, or a price you should copy onto a contract without checking it against your own crew and invoices.

Common questions

Should I match a competitor's price if my job is stain-grade?

Not without checking the scope the competitor's number was priced for first. On this calculator's own default crew rates, 80 linear feet walks away at $1,182.95 as paint-grade simple cove in one flat 8-ft room, and at $7,710.87 as stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story cathedral foyer with an LED cove -- the same footage, a $6,527.92 gap. A quote a homeowner is holding almost always describes the first job. Matching it on the second means absorbing that gap yourself.

What is the extra-work share, and why does it matter more than the linear-foot price?

It is the share of crew hours that come from corners, ceiling shape, access, demo, blocking, an LED cove, and casing match -- everything a flat per-foot rate cannot see, because it is not linear feet. On this calculator's worked examples, that share is 21.4% of crew hours on the cheap paint-grade special and 60.2% on the stain-grade built-up foyer, using the identical 80 feet of crown. A per-foot price only ever describes the run; the extra-work share is what is actually different between two jobs that quote the same length.

How much of the gap is invisible to a per-foot number?

On this calculator's own four preset jobs, the extra-work share of crew hours runs 21.4% (cheap paint-grade special), 20.6% (typical colonial), 48.6% (stain-grade colonial in a tray ceiling), and 60.2% (stain-grade built-up in a cathedral foyer). A linear-foot price cannot move with any of that -- it moves only with linear feet, which is identical in the first and last row.

vs-a-flat-rate-crown-molding-special.htm.text:
← Crown Molding Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat "$8 a foot" crown molding special

"$8 a foot installed crown" is not a price for a crown molding install — it is a price for one specific grade, one profile, and one flat ceiling, quietly applied to every room the truck pulls up to.

What a flat "$8 a foot" special is

A flat per-foot rate is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard or a website, multiplied by a tape measurement. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match on their own dining room.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually the cheapest profile (paint-grade simple cove, mitered and caulked), the cheapest ceiling (flat, stepladder access), no coping, no stacked pieces, no scaffold — and then reused for every crown run afterward, whether or not the next room looks anything like the one the rate was set on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the linear feet, inside and outside corners, room count, and travel, plus grade (paint or stain), profile (simple cove, colonial, or built-up), ceiling shape (flat, cathedral, or tray), and height/access (standard, tall, or a two-story foyer), along with extras such as demo of existing crown, blocking, an LED cove, and matching casing. It prices the run, the corners, the grade, the ceiling, and the access separately, and returns a walk-away price and extra-work share below which the job loses money — for this room, not a generic one.

Job$8/ft quoteWalk-away priceVerdict
Cheap special: 80 lf paint-grade simple cove, 8 insides, one flat 8-ft room$640.00$1,182.95Short $542.95
Typical colonial: 180 lf paint-grade, 16 insides, 3 rooms$1,440.00$3,302.54Short $1,862.54
Losing job: 80 lf stain-grade built-up, two-story cathedral foyer, LED cove$640.00$7,710.87Short $7,070.87

Worked using this calculator's own starting kits at a $42 crew wage, 32% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 20% target margin — the form's own defaults, not a number invented for this page. Open the calculator's presets to check any row yourself.

What a flat per-foot special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same per-foot rate whether the job is paint-grade simple cove in a flat room or stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story cathedral foyer — several times the labor and material for the same linear footage. Prices the run from the entered grade, profile, ceiling shape, and height, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "crown molding" as one mitered run, with no separate line for coping stain-grade insides, stacking a built-up profile, a spring-angle change at a shaped ceiling, or setting a scaffold in a two-story foyer. Times the corners, the stacked pieces, the ceiling shape, and the access as their own extra-work hours, so that work shows up instead of being absorbed into the per-foot rate or skipped.
Assumes flat-ceiling, stepladder access with no demo, blocking, LED cove, or casing match, so a cathedral foyer, an LED reveal, or a casing-match order gets quoted the same as a run that needs none of that. Adds demo, blocking, LED, and casing-match hours and material only for what was entered, so the two jobs price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "per-foot rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the carpenter a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when an owner asks to match a cheaper per-foot bid on a stain-grade built-up job. Reports the walk-away price and the extra-work share of the job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the carpenter commits to it.

A flat per-foot special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat "$8 a foot" crown molding special get the price wrong?

Because the labor and material scale with the grade, the profile, the ceiling shape, and the access, not with linear feet alone. Paint-grade simple cove in one flat 8-ft room is a different job from stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story cathedral foyer with fourteen coped inside corners and an LED cove. A flat per-foot rate quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat per-foot rate usually leave out entirely?

The corners, the coping, the ceiling, and the ladder. A published per-foot price is set on the cheapest run it was ever quoted against — paint-grade, mitered, flat ceiling, a stepladder — and has nowhere to put the hours for coped stain-grade insides, stacked built-up pieces, a spring-angle change at a cathedral ceiling, or a rolling scaffold in a two-story foyer. A carpenter pricing off the per-foot rate alone is short before the miter saw comes out of the truck.

How much do grade, profile, ceiling, and access actually add over the per-foot rate?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $42 crew wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin: 80 linear feet of paint-grade simple cove in one flat room walks away at $1,182.95, against an $8/ft quote of $640.00 — already $542.95 short. The identical 80 linear feet as stain-grade built-up crown in a two-story cathedral foyer with an LED cove walks away at $7,710.87 against the same $640.00 quote — $7,070.87 short, thirteen times worse on the same footage. 180 linear feet of paint-grade colonial across three rooms walks away at $3,302.54, $1,862.54 over its $1,440.00 quote. Grade, profile, ceiling, and height move the number far more than linear feet alone.

Is a flat per-foot rate ever the right way to quote crown molding?

For the one job it was actually priced on — paint-grade simple cove, mitered and caulked, a flat ceiling, a stepladder, no demo, no blocking, no LED cove, no casing match — a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers it does. The risk is applying it to a stain-grade or built-up job, a shaped ceiling, or a two-story access without noticing, because the per-foot rate does not know which job it is looking at and neither does the carpenter until the corners are cut.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the linear feet, corners, grade, profile, ceiling shape, height, and extras, plus your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price and extra-work share for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat "$8 a foot" special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. Homewyse

Homewyse prices a crown-molding install from a zip code and a linear-foot count alone. This page is a free, private worksheet for the same question with the grade, profile, ceiling, and corners put back in — the inputs a zip-and-footage estimate has no field for.
